title: Ang 1167: Ravidas in Bhairao
tomorrow: the morning raga is done. what does spring sound like?

lines: A PARADE OF THINGS TO WANT.
SEE IT, WANT IT, IT'S GONE.
cards: Every scroll through a feed is a little parade of things to want: a jacket, a trip, a face, a life. You see it, and the wanting starts. Then the next post, and that one's gone.
On ang 1167, the last hymn in Bhairao, Ravidas names that exact loop in two lines, and then asks the question it leaves behind. If everything you can see is passing, what's worth longing for?

teach.b: In paraphrase, Ravidas opens: without seeing, longing doesn't arise.
And whatever is seen will pass away. That's the feed in one breath.

teach.h: TURN THE LONGING TO THE NAME.
teach.b: Then his answer: the one who repeats the Name, Naam, with praise is the real yogi, free of wanting. So the longing doesn't get switched off. It gets turned.
Away from what's seen and passing, toward the Name, which the eyes can't scroll past. That's how the morning raga ends: not with a rule against wanting, but with a better thing to want.
Here's a neighbor who says something close.
Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, in the King James Bible: "for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal."

The shared part is real: both say the seen is passing, and both point the heart past it. The difference is real too. For Paul, the unseen hope runs through Jesus, raised from the dead, as the same chapter says.
For Ravidas, it's the Name, repeated and dwelt on, here, now. Two neighbors looking the same direction, each through their own window.

how: Ravidas's hymns are sung in kirtan as part of the Guru Granth Sahib; his hymn at ang 1167 is the last in raga Bhairao, and readers turn from it straight into Basant.

o: where the spring raga Basant begins
where Ravidas closes Bhairao: what is seen will pass
where Namdev begs the Lord to drink his milk

games.q: the seen and the unseen — tap the pairs.

s: Ravidas says longing is always wrong
he says longing comes from seeing, and what's seen passes; then he turns it toward the Name.
a line in Paul's letters also says what is seen is temporary
2 Corinthians 4:18, in the King James Bible: the things which are seen are temporal.
Ravidas and Paul are saying exactly the same thing
both say the seen passes; Paul's hope runs through Jesus raised, Ravidas's through the Name.

games.q: your phone dies and takes years of photos with it. a friend shrugs: "see, that's why nothing matters." what would Ravidas's hymn say back?
o: what's seen passes, so something should matter more: he points the longing at the Name.
he'd agree: since everything passes, nothing is worth caring about at all.
he'd say longing is the real problem, so stop wanting anything.
games.why: Ravidas doesn't end at 'it all passes.' he ends with a better thing to long for: the Name, repeated with praise.

practice: Close your eyes. Everything you could look at is still there; for two minutes, you're not looking at any of it. Follow the breath, which you can't see either.
If you pray, you can let the word Waheguru ride on it. If you'd like, read ang 1167 before you begin.
